cells.tense: You are here with the pen, seeing the shape a thing makes once its details fall away.
cells.ask: Explain one pattern you have spotted to someone who did not see it, in plain words, and stop when they have it.
cells.core: You can look at something messy and see the shape it makes. Not the details — what is underneath them, the way this works the same way that does. That is not a trick you learned. It comes from actually understanding the thing, or it does not come at all.\n\nAnd what you see frees people when you say it. Something that looked fixed turns out to have room in it, and you are the one who points at the room. That is the balance: the pattern is real, and you are here, using it. The cost is that clarity invites you to keep going past the point anyone needed. Hand over the shape once, then let it be used.
cells.sheetLine: You see the shape underneath, and you say it plainly.
cells.verb: to see the pattern stripped clean of the thing it was made of
cells.place: becoming what you are, without dimming or distortion

cells.tense: Somewhere ahead you are bracing for the pattern to turn, and you are already checking for the turn.
cells.ask: Write one rule you keep checking against, then follow it for a day without adding a second.
cells.core: The pattern-seeing has stopped taking a break. You look at a nice evening and find the machinery in it. You look at a kind word and find the reason behind it. Every shape you spot now comes with the next one, and the next one is worse than the last. Nothing gets to be just what it is for long.\n\nThe trouble is not that the reading is wrong. Some of it lands. The trouble is that there is no end to the reading, and the end is where you would get to be present. You do not need more depth here. You need one structure you will actually stand on — a rule, a time, a form — so there is something solid under you instead of another layer. Build that, and the clarity has somewhere to rest.
cells.sheetLine: You are reading the machinery so hard you cannot be in the room.

cells.tense: You left a doorway behind you and are still standing where it used to be.
cells.ask: Ask one person to tell you the history of something they do, and listen without deciding whether it is true.
cells.core: When something has a surface, you take it as the whole thing. A story is just what happened. A habit is just what you do. Anything further in feels like someone trying to sell you something. You are not shallow — the depth is there — but you have stopped letting yourself reach for it.\n\nWhat you are missing is not insight. It is the ground that insight grows out of: shared ways of holding meaning, passed from people who came before. You cannot force your way into that by trying harder. It comes back by spending time with what other people have carried, and letting it be worth something before you understand it. Start with one thing you have been treating as only itself.
cells.sheetLine: You take the surface as the whole thing because depth stopped being safe.

cells.tense: You are already shaping what happens next here, and you have not said so to yourself.
cells.ask: Name one agreement you keep obeying, and tell the person it came from that you are changing it.
cells.core: You know what pattern you are in. You can describe the arrangement clearly, from a distance, as if it were a fact about how things are. What you have not done is add up that you are the one standing inside it, making it hold. You talk about how things work as though the working were happening on its own.\n\nThat is not a failure of insight. It is a missing sentence about who is holding the pen. The pattern is not a fact about the world. It is a thing you are doing — seeing it, keeping it going, agreeing to it. Say that part out loud once, about one arrangement that has been running you, and the pattern becomes something you can pick up instead of something that picks you.
cells.sheetLine: You can see the pattern, but not that you are the one keeping it.
cells.verb: to see the pattern stripped clean of the thing it was made of

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person treats patterns as binding rules, or that seeing patterns has stopped liberating them — the record gives the capacity, not its history or its effects. A reader could object that of course they know pattern binds them, or that they find pattern useful, not a prison. The asks survive being wrong because they are small, external, and do not depend on my read of the interior: reading something through, saying an agreement aloud, explaining a habit to one person, all still work if the person is doing fine. The sentence that serves me rather than them is any line that congratulates the reader on being good at abstraction; I have cut every one.
